problems.slice:
What causes it

A slice starts left and curves right for a right-hander. The cause is almost always a clubface that is open to the swing path at impact, and a path that cuts across the ball from outside to inside. A weak grip, an open stance and an over-the-top move from the top all feed it.

How golfers fix it

The most recommended help is Hank Haney's live lesson on Performance Golf, Hank Haney Fixes A High Handicapper's Slice LIVE, recommended by 11 golfers, 7 of whom say it fixed their slice. He links the slice to an open face and an over-the-top move. Rick Shiels' complete slice guide, recommended by 9 golfers, works through causes and fixes in order. Golfers commonly work on:

  • A neutral or slightly stronger grip so the face can close.
  • Shallowing the club in transition so it approaches from the inside.
  • Checking shoulder alignment and trail forearm position at setup, as Danny Maude suggests.

Common mistakes

Trying to swing harder to "fix" the curve usually makes it worse. Another common error is aiming well left and swinging across the line, which keeps the out-to-in path alive. Changing only the grip without addressing the path can swap a slice for a pull, so give each change a few range sessions before judging it.
problems.hook:
What causes it

A hook curves hard left for a right-hander. The face is closed relative to the path at impact, which is often caused by a very strong grip, an over-active release of the hands, or a path that is far too inside-out. Sometimes it is a reaction to years of fighting a slice, where the golfer has over-corrected the grip and release.

How golfers fix it

Few golfers have reported fixing a hook with video so far, and the data is thin. Rick Shiels' 5 Simple Ways To Fix Your Golf Hook, recommended by 2 golfers who both say it helped, begins with grip changes. Other recommended clips look at the takeaway, since an overly inside move can load the path too far from the inside. Typical fixes include:

  • Weakening the lead-hand grip until you see about two knuckles.
  • Quieting the hands through impact rather than flipping them over.
  • Fixing an inside takeaway, as in the Justin Rose and Nelly Korda drills golfers recommend.

Common mistakes

Aiming the body far right to allow for the hook only makes the swing more inside-out. Weakening the grip too much overnight can flip you straight into a slice, so make small changes. Also avoid trying to hold the face open by force, which tires the hands and tends to come undone under pressure.
problems.shank:
What causes it

A shank sends the ball off the hosel and sharply right. The clubhead is too far out toward the toe line at impact, usually because your body moves toward the ball in the downswing, or because the handle is pushed out and the face is open.

How golfers fix it

Paul Wilson's How to Stop Shanking in 5 Minutes, recommended by 6 golfers with 4 saying it fixed their shanks, gives a three-point fix that includes standing taller and adjusting your setup. Golficity's quick drill, recommended by 3 golfers, all of whom say it worked, uses a change of perspective to retrain where the club arrives. Common fixes are:

  • Standing a little further from the ball with balance toward the heels.
  • Keeping your chest and hips back instead of lunging toward the ball.
  • Placing a headcover or ball outside the target ball and missing it.

Common mistakes

Panicking and trying to change everything at once is the biggest trap. Many golfers also grip down and crowd the ball, which makes the shank worse. Do not practice with the same club until it settles; switch to a different club, slow the swing and rebuild feel for the centre of the face.
problems.fat_thin:
What causes it

Fat shots hit the ground before the ball and thin shots catch it too high on the face. Both come from the lowest point of the swing being in the wrong place. The usual reasons are hanging back on the trail foot, losing posture so the club bottoms out early, or scooping at the ball to lift it. Poor balance and tempo also move the low point around.

How golfers fix it

Golfers have not yet reached a strong consensus on a single video here, but two are worth noting. Bryson DeChambeau's lesson to Rick Shiels, recommended by 4 golfers, covers low point and release timing for iron strike. KraftyGolf's slow motion clip, also recommended by 4 golfers, shows what fat contact looks like and why a hitting mat can hide it. Ways golfers improve:

  • Move pressure into the lead foot through impact.
  • Draw a line on the ground and aim to strike just ahead of it.
  • Practice on turf, not a forgiving mat.

Common mistakes

Trying to help the ball into the air is the classic error, because it moves the low point backward. Another is staring at the ball and freezing the body rather than rotating through. Do not judge your strike on mats only; they let you hit fat shots that would cost you distance on grass.
problems.iron_contact:
What causes it

Good iron compression means hitting the ball first, then the turf, with the shaft leaning toward the target at impact. Weak, high shots usually come from the opposite: the handle is behind the clubhead, the wrists flip and the club scoops. Staying on the trail side, losing pressure in the lead foot and casting early all rob you of compression.

How golfers fix it

DSTGolf's long video, recommended by 12 golfers with 2 saying it helped, challenges myths about impact positions and angles. Bryson DeChambeau's lesson to Rick Shiels, recommended by 11 golfers and 3 who say it fixed things, teaches a drill for iron strike. Danny Maude's live lesson on trail arm and wrist pressure is recommended by 9 golfers, and Athletic Motion Golf explains how tour players get shaft lean through hand position and rotation rather than pushing, also recommended by 9. Common work includes:

  • Shifting pressure forward before the club arrives.
  • Keeping the lead wrist flat or slightly bowed.
  • Rotating through so the hands lead.

Common mistakes

Pushing the hands forward at address and then still flipping at impact does nothing. Another error is trying to hit down by dropping the shoulder, which leads to chunks. Compression comes from sequence and pressure, not from forcing a steep angle.
problems.early_extension:
What causes it

Early extension means your hips move toward the ball in the downswing and your pelvis loses its posture angle. It forces you to stand up, squeeze the arms and then either flip or block the club. Causes include weak glutes, tight hips, setting up too close to the ball and a downswing that does not rotate the pelvis.

How golfers fix it

Athletic Motion Golf's Pros vs. Ams hip rotation video is recommended by 39 golfers, 6 of whom say it helped. It shows how the lower body sequences in a swing that avoids early extension. Their follow up on clearing the hips has 22 recommendations. Eric Cogorno's Fix Early Extension FAST gives a simple drill to keep the hips back, recommended by 16 golfers. Popular fixes include:

  • A chair or wall behind your glutes to keep your pelvis back.
  • Pushing into the ground with the lead foot so the hips turn rather than slide.
  • Stand slightly further from the ball with good knee flex.

Common mistakes

Golfers often try to hold their hips back so stiffly that the swing becomes blocked and the arms get stuck. The goal is rotation, not freezing. Also avoid fixing it by standing further away than your reach allows; that only trades one fault for another.
problems.over_the_top:
What causes it

Over the top means the club moves outward and steeply from the top, then cuts across the ball. It produces pulls, slices and the occasional fat shot. Common causes are starting the downswing with the shoulders or arms, an inside takeaway that you correct with a loop, and a backswing that is too long for your mobility.

How golfers fix it

Justin Rose's feel versus real drill from PGA Tour is the standout, recommended by 22 golfers with 3 saying it fixed their over-the-top move; it works on hand path and sequencing. Jim Waldron's Arm Swing Illusion has 16 recommendations for keeping arms and chest working together. Athletic Motion Golf's shallowing video, recommended by 12 golfers, compares pro and amateur transitions. Titleist's explainer is also recommended by 15. Golfers work on:

  • Starting the downswing with the lower body.
  • Letting the trail elbow drop toward the hip.
  • Feeling the club drop behind you before you turn.

Common mistakes

Swinging from the inside by force makes a block or hook. Another mistake is working on the transition without checking the takeaway, which may be the real cause. Slow-motion reps help far more than hitting balls at full speed with the same pattern. Finally, a steep shoulder turn at the top can cause the same move, so check that your torso turns around your spine and not tilts upward.
problems.casting_lag:
What causes it

Casting is releasing the wrist angle early from the top, so the club head speed is spent before impact. It costs distance and leads to scooping and thin shots. It is typically caused by starting the downswing with the arms, grabbing the grip too tightly, or trying to help the ball into the air.

How golfers fix it

Monte Scheinblum's No Turn Cast Swing Drill is recommended by 11 golfers, 2 of whom say it fixed their casting; it helps you feel wrist hinge. Danny Maude's live lesson on trail arm and wrist pressure is recommended by 9. Clay Ballard's lag drill, recommended by 8 golfers, teaches free-floating lag and tempo. Common ways to work on it:

  • Make small swings that keep the angle until the hands pass the trail leg.
  • Hold the club lightly so the wrists can stay loaded.
  • Use the lower body to start the downswing so the arms follow.

Common mistakes

Trying to hold the angle by tensing the forearms makes it worse. The angle should be held by sequence, not strength. Also avoid copying a late hit by flipping at the last moment, which is the opposite fix.
problems.sway_weight_shift:
What causes it

A sway slides the body away from the target in the backswing, and hanging back leaves too much weight on the trail side in the downswing. The result is fat shots, thin shots and a loss of power. Reverse pivots, locked trail knees and an unstable base are the usual causes. Poor footwork is also a factor. Rolling onto the outside of the trail foot, or lifting the lead heel too early, lets the body slide instead of turning around a stable centre.

How golfers fix it

Athletic Motion Golf's How To Shift Weight & Pressure Like A Pro is recommended by 23 golfers, using data on how pros move pressure from trail to lead. Padraig Harrington's hip clearing tip is recommended by 19, with 5 saying it helped. The Chasing Scratch podcast on using the lead foot is recommended by 15. Ways golfers improve:

  • Keep the trail knee flexed and let the hips turn instead of slide.
  • Press into the lead foot at the start of the downswing.
  • Use a step drill to match weight shift with rotation.

Common mistakes

Do not go to the opposite extreme and shift your weight so far forward that you cannot turn. Another error is thinking of weight transfer as a lateral slide when it is really pressure moving while the body rotates.
problems.takeaway_backswing:
What causes it

The first move of the swing sets club path, face angle, width and turn. Errors such as an inside takeaway, an arms-only lift or a rolled-open face tend to need later compensations. A backswing that is too long or disconnected is also common among amateurs. Many golfers also confuse width with reach. A wide backswing comes from turning the body and keeping the arms in front of the chest, not from pushing the hands away from the body.

How golfers fix it

Jim Waldron's The Arm Swing Illusion is the clear favourite with 162 recommendations and 28 golfers saying it fixed something, explaining why the arms should not drive the backswing. RollYourRock's Faldo pre-set drill is recommended by 37 golfers for a good top position. Danny Maude's takeaway drill, recommended by 29, leads with the shoulders. Athletic Motion Golf's shoulder rotation and arm depth video has 25. Golfers focus on:

  • Turning the chest and arms together.
  • Keeping the trail arm connected, as the towel drill teaches.
  • Building a full turn before lifting the arms.

Common mistakes

Over-thinking a takeaway position often creates tension. Also avoid pulling the club inside on purpose, which leads to the over-the-top move. Check it on video from face-on and down-the-line.
problems.transition_downswing:
What causes it

The transition is the moment the swing changes direction. What moves first and how the club drops into the slot decide the path. Arms starting before the lower body, a lunging upper body and a steep shaft all cause over-the-top moves and inconsistency.

How golfers fix it

Justin Rose's feel versus real drill from PGA Tour is recommended by 46 golfers, 3 of whom say it fixed their transition. Athletic Motion Golf's shallowing video has 24 recommendations. TEE FLIP GOLF's short clip on Bryson DeChambeau's advice is recommended by 11. Fixes include:

  • Let the lower body start the downswing.
  • Feel the trail elbow move in front of the trail hip.
  • Pause briefly at the top in slow practice.

Tigerswoodyshow's Butch Harmon and Tiger Woods clip, recommended by 12 golfers, adds a drill that keeps the arms from beating the hips. Use these ideas to build a slow-motion routine, then add speed.

Common mistakes

Rushing from the top is the most common mistake. Another is exaggerating the drop so far inside that you get stuck and flip. Learn the feel with half swings first, then speed it up.
problems.rotation_hips:
What causes it

The hips turn and clear in the downswing so the arms and club can swing through. When they stall, the arms take over, you lose room and often fall into early extension or a block. Limited hip mobility and a lack of lead-side stability are frequent culprits. Even a golfer with a good setup can stall if the lead leg does not firm up. A loose lead knee lets the pelvis slide instead of turning, and the arms then have no room to swing through, so the club gets stuck behind the body.

How golfers fix it

Athletic Motion Golf's Pros vs. Ams video is the leading recommendation with 79 golfers and 6 saying it helped. Padraig Harrington's tip on clearing the pelvis has 48 recommendations, using footwork and loading the lead leg. Athletic Motion's Clearing The Hips video has 32, and Jim Waldron's Arm Swing Illusion has 29. Common work:

  • Load the lead leg and turn the belt buckle toward the target.
  • Let the trail heel come off as the body rotates.
  • Add hip mobility work off the course.

Common mistakes

Spinning the hips out too early leaves the club behind. Another mistake is sliding rather than rotating. Do not try to force turn beyond your range; that creates a sway or lifts the head.
problems.release_clubface:
What causes it

The release is how the face rotates through impact, and it has more influence on starting direction than any other factor. Too little rotation leaves the face open; too much closes it. Grip, wrist action and arm rotation all play a part. The face also depends on the face angle at the top and on how the lead wrist is set during the backswing. A cupped lead wrist tends to leave the face open, while a very bowed one tends to leave it closed, so release problems often start long before impact.

How golfers fix it

Danny Maude's live lesson on trail arm and wrist pressure is recommended by 26 golfers, 3 of whom say it fixed their release. Padraig Harrington's Squaring the Clubface has 12 recommendations, as it explains why most bad shots come from the face. Athletic Motion Golf's release video has 10, and Harrington's piece on active wrists has 10. Typical fixes:

  • Soften your grip pressure.
  • Let the forearms rotate naturally as the body turns.
  • Check face angle at the top.

Common mistakes

Forcing the release with the hands creates hooks and pulls. Holding the face open creates blocks and slices. Do not copy the wrist action of a tour player without matching the body motion.
problems.grip:
What causes it

Your grip decides how easily the face can square at impact. A grip that is too weak, too strong, too tight or held in the palms tends to bring slices, hooks and a loss of feel. Hand position often connects to setup and posture. Grip pressure matters as much as grip position. Squeezing tightly locks the wrists and forearms, which blocks the natural rotation of the face and costs speed, while a grip that is too loose lets the club twist at impact.

How golfers fix it

Golf Channel's How to Properly Grip Your Golf Club is recommended by 26 golfers, 5 of whom say it fixed things, with simple steps for beginners. Padraig Harrington's A Proper Grip has 25 recommendations, and his follow up on placing the fingers has 24. Meandmygolf's video on grip mistakes has 17. Golfers often work on:

  • Holding the club in the fingers of the lead hand.
  • Seeing two knuckles at address.
  • Light pressure, about a 4 out of 10.

Meandmygolf links grip to takeaway and posture, which is useful: a good hold on the club makes the rest of the swing easier to build.

Common mistakes

Squeezing harder for control is the usual mistake. Another is changing grip without changing the swing, then judging it after a few shots. Give a new grip time to feel normal.
problems.setup_posture:
What causes it

Stance width, ball position, spine angle and alignment decide what is possible before the club moves. Poor setups such as standing too far away, a rounded back or aiming left build compensation into the swing. Posture also affects how well you can rotate. Too much knee bend or a rounded upper back limits turn, while standing too tall forces the arms to reach, and either one can show up later as early extension or a loss of balance.

How golfers fix it

Athletic Motion Golf's Pros vs. Ams video is recommended by 25 golfers, 5 of whom say it helped. Their video on how far to stand from the ball has 24. George Gankas' complete guide to golf setup has 16, covering posture and weight distribution, and Athletic Motion's address video has 15. Common fixes:

  • Hinge from the hips with a flat back.
  • Let the arms hang freely.
  • Check alignment with a club on the ground.

Common mistakes

Overthinking a stiff, robotic setup is common. Another is copying a tour player's open stance without their mobility. Check your setup on video regularly. Also remember that setup is not fixed; it changes with club length. Drivers need a wider stance and more tilt than wedges, so check each one rather than copying a single position for everything.
problems.driver_distance:
What causes it

The driver is different from your irons: a sweeping, upward strike with a wide stance, forward ball position and tee height all matter. Lost distance often comes from a downward attack, poor face control and mis-hits low on the face. Tee height and ball position matter more than most golfers realise. A ball teed too low encourages a steep strike that adds backspin and robs carry, while one too far back reduces launch. Many slicers also lose distance because the open face adds sidespin and leaks speed.

How golfers fix it

Bryson DeChambeau's How To Swing A Driver is recommended by 9 golfers, 2 of whom say it helped, with his crack-the-whip feel. Rick Shiels' How to hit Golf driver Long & Straight has 7, with 4 saying it helped, covering ball position, posture and setup. Rory McIlroy's setup lesson from Fore Play Golf has 5. Typical changes:

  • Tee the ball so half of it sits above the crown.
  • Position the ball off the lead heel.
  • Tilt the spine away from the target.

Common mistakes

Swinging as hard as possible usually costs centre strikes. Another error is aiming to lift the ball, which creates a steep path. Fix path and strike before chasing speed.
problems.wedges_pitching:
What causes it

Partial wedges from 30 to 100 yards need distance control, clean contact and a repeatable length of swing. Errors come from decelerating, scooping or changing wrist action on every shot. Distance control is mostly about repeating the same length and tempo of swing. Golfers who change grip pressure, wrist action or how far they take the club back on every shot get random results, even with a good strike. Poor ball position and weight too far back also send contact behind the ball.

How golfers fix it

Rick Shiels' This Golf Lesson Changed my LIFE! is recommended by 5 golfers, with 2 saying it helped, covering technique and bounce. Phil Mickelson's Chipping 101 and Short Game Secrets each have 3 recommendations and all 3 golfers say they helped. Dan Grieve's pitch shot video has 4, with a stock 60 yard wedge. Golfers work on:

  • A clock system for swing length.
  • A narrow stance with weight slightly forward.
  • Letting the bounce glide through the turf.

Common mistakes

Decelerating into the ball is the most common mistake. Another is using full swings with soft wedges and hoping the ball lands right. Learn three carry distances first. Track your carry distances with three swing lengths and write them down; that notebook is worth more than any swing tip when you are 60 yards from the pin.
problems.chipping:
What causes it

Chipping uses short strokes around the green, and the common problems are fat and thin contact, deceleration and the yips. They stem from poor weight placement, flipping wrists and a lack of commitment. The yips are a separate problem. Tense hands and a fear of a bad result make some golfers jab at the ball, and no amount of technique helps until the stroke feels calm again. Simplifying the motion and choosing a lower-lofted club often takes pressure off.

How golfers fix it

Phil Mickelson's Chipping 101 from Foresight Golf is the top pick, recommended by 23 golfers, 12 of whom say it helped. His longer lesson, The Art of Chipping, has 13. Kevin Kisner's lesson on body connection has 9, and Rick Shiels' chipping lesson has 7 with 4 saying it fixed their chipping. Common advice:

  • Lean the weight onto the lead foot.
  • Keep the hands ahead of the clubhead.
  • Turn your chest through the shot.

Common mistakes

Trying to scoop the ball up is the main error. Another is changing your technique for each lie. Choose a simple method and use less loft when possible. Also resist practicing from perfect lies only. Most chips in a round are not ideal, so spend part of your session on rough, slopes and tight turf.
problems.putting:
What causes it

Putting problems come from the stroke, speed control or green reading. Poor setup, deceleration and a nervous, tight grip can each lead to misses and three-putts. Speed matters more than line for most amateurs. A putter that arrives with an open or closed face, or one that decelerates through the ball, sends putts offline and short. Eyes not over the ball and a grip that is too tense both make the stroke less repeatable.

How golfers fix it

Data on putting is thin so far. Porzak Golf's Last Putting Lesson You Will Ever Need has 3 recommendations, covering seven tips on stroke and setup. Paul Wilson's putting tip has 3, using a wiggle drill and reset routine for yips. Jerome Rufin's twelve tips have 2. Golfers often practice:

  • Gate drills for a square face.
  • Ladder drills for speed control.
  • A consistent pre-putt routine.

Common mistakes

Focusing on line while ignoring speed is common. Another is changing putters constantly. Judge progress using putts holed from 3 to 6 feet. Golfers also make the mistake of reading greens only once they stand over the ball; walk up from behind and look at the slope from the low side as well.
problems.speed_training:
What causes it

Clubhead speed depends on the sequence of the body, wrist hinge and how well you use the ground. Lack of mobility, early casting and arm-only swings limit it. Speed also depends on how well you use the ground and how freely you let the club swing. Many golfers chase speed by tensing their arms, but fast swings usually come from relaxed hands, a good turn and a well-timed push into the lead side.

How golfers fix it

Bryson DeChambeau's driver swing walkthrough is recommended by 4 golfers, 2 of whom say it helped. Athletic Motion Golf's club head speed video also has 4, focusing on hand speed and holding wrist hinge. Titleist's vertical jump drill has 4, and Dr Kwon's rope swing drill has 3. Golfers try:

  • Jump drills to train ground force.
  • Rope swings to feel throwing motion.
  • Light overspeed swings, built up gradually.

Common mistakes

Swinging harder without sequence adds tension and misses. Another mistake is skipping warm-ups. Build speed gradually and keep centre strikes. Warm up before any overspeed work, and allow recovery between sessions. If your back or elbows hurt, back off and see a coach or physio.
problems.mobility_fitness:
What causes it

Flexibility and strength decide which positions you can reach. Limited hips, thoracic spine or shoulders force swing compensations. A lack of rotation in the thoracic spine, hip internal rotation or ankle mobility is a common reason a swing looks stuck. Core and glute strength matter too, because they stabilise the body while the arms swing. Without them, golfers sway, lose posture or lift their head at impact.

How golfers fix it

Yoga With Adriene's yoga for golfers is recommended by 7 golfers, building flexibility and core rotation. Jonathan Kim-Moss explains how posture affects the swing and back, and Malaska Golf offers a pre-round warm up, each with 2. Golfers do:

  • Hip and thoracic rotation drills.
  • Core and glute work.
  • A short warm-up before play.

Iona Stephen's TPI session shows a longer assessment of hip movement and ground power, which is worth watching if you want to know where your own limits are.

Common mistakes

Skipping fitness until pain appears is common. Another is stretching cold muscles aggressively. Build a short routine you can repeat. Also remember that fitness helps golf only if you keep it up. A shorter routine done three times a week beats one huge session that you never repeat.
problems.practice_method:
What causes it

Practice helps when it is structured. Hitting balls without a target, feedback or a plan builds habits and does not change them. Feedback matters as much as repetition. Without a camera, a launch monitor or a coach, golfers can repeat the same fault for years while feeling that they are improving. Random shots with no target also fail to prepare you for the course.

How golfers fix it

RollYourRock's Faldo pre-set drill is recommended by 23 golfers, 5 saying it helped. Justin Rose's feel versus real drill has 19. GOLFTEC's towel drill has 17 and Titleist's step drill has 13. Golfers practice by:

  • Using one drill per session.
  • Filming swings.
  • Alternating drill reps and real shots.

Common mistakes

Changing many things at once is common. Another mistake is not testing on the course. Keep notes on what works. Finish each session with a few shots played as if on the course, with a full routine and a specific target, so you check that the change transfers. Setting a simple target for each drill, such as hitting five solid shots in a row, keeps the work honest.
problems.course_management:
What causes it

Course management is choosing targets and clubs that fit your actual dispersion. Poor decisions cost more strokes than most swing flaws. Most golfers have a normal miss, such as a fade or a pull, and a limited range of distances. Good strategy accepts that pattern and aims to keep the ball in play, rather than aiming straight at every flag and relying on a perfect swing.

How golfers fix it

Golf Digest's The Clever Aiming Strategy is recommended by 8 golfers, explaining aiming for your typical misses. Golf Sidekick's How to Break 100 has 5 with 1 saying it helped. Their other videos have 2. Golfers:

  • Aim at the middle of the green.
  • Pick the safe side of hazards.
  • Take enough club.

Common mistakes

Hero shots after a bad one are the usual mistake. Another is ignoring your real carry numbers. Keep it simple. Write down your real carry distances and miss patterns after a few rounds; they will tell you where to aim more clearly than guesswork does.
problems.mental:
What causes it

The mental game covers routines, pressure and staying out of your own way. Tension, overthinking and rushing wreck technique that works on the range. The brain also fights new moves under pressure. Golfers who have just changed something in the swing tend to fall back on old habits when a shot matters, and that tension shows in grip, tempo and breathing.

How golfers fix it

Data is limited. Paul Wilson's putting tip has 2 recommendations, with a reset routine for yips. Danny Maude's iron striking basics also has 2, simplifying swing thoughts. Golfers:

  • Use a pre-shot routine.
  • Pick one swing thought.
  • Breathe out before the shot.

Treat the mental side as a skill you practice: a routine on the range, a reset after a bad shot, and one clear target for each swing.

Common mistakes

Chasing perfect swings on the course is the main mistake. Another is dwelling on bad shots. Move on quickly. A routine you can repeat in any situation is worth more than clever mental tricks, and takes minutes a week to build.
problems.fundamentals_general:
What causes it

Swing fundamentals tie the pieces together: grip, setup, turn, sequence and impact. Most faults trace back to one or two basics. Most of the swing models golfers learn are simplifications. Good coaches help you decide which piece is limiting you, rather than adding more. Often it is a setup issue or the way the arms and body work together.

How golfers fix it

Jim Waldron's The Arm Swing Illusion is recommended by 87 golfers, 18 saying it fixed something. Jerome Rufin's lesson has 16, with 4 fixed. DSTGolf has 15 and the Arm Swing Illusion Introduction has 14. Golfers work on:

  • Connected arms and chest.
  • A balanced finish.
  • One fault at a time.

Common mistakes

Collecting tips without a plan is common. Another is changing too fast. Pick one source and stay with it. Film yourself once a month so you can see whether you are really changing, rather than relying on feel alone. Keep notes on what you changed and how the ball flight responded, so you can tell what is working and drop what is not. Slow progress on one fundamental beats fast churn through ten.

guide_coaches.title: The best golf instruction channels on YouTube, ranked by golfers
guide_coaches.description: The top 15 golf YouTube channels ranked by how many golfers independently recommended them on Reddit, not by subscriber counts.
guide_coaches.html:
How we rank golf instruction channels

Most lists of the best golf channels sort by subscribers or views. Those numbers tell you who is popular, not who helps. GolfVotes counts something different: how many golfers on Reddit independently recommended a specific YouTube lesson when somebody asked for help with their game. A recommendation means a golfer put their name to a video in a public thread. When golfers go further and say a video actually fixed their problem, we count that as a fix.

Below are the top 15 channels, ranked by total independent recommendations across all of their videos. The number of videos shows how widely a channel is cited, and the fix count shows how often golfers credit it with real change.

The top 15 channels

  1. Athletic Motion Golf – Recommended by 1408 golfers across 220 videos, with 74 reporting a fix. Golfers recommend it for takeaway and backswing, hip rotation and transition, and keep coming back to its pros-versus-amateurs comparisons.
  2. Porzak Golf – Recommended by 581 golfers across 136 videos, with 46 reporting a fix. Golfers recommend it for takeaway, transition and setup fundamentals.
  3. Danny Maude – Recommended by 551 golfers across 97 videos, with 101 reporting a fix. Golfers recommend it for swing fundamentals, takeaway and setup. Golfers credit his videos with fixing a problem more often than any other channel, with 101 fixes reported.
  4. Eric Cogorno Golf – Recommended by 491 golfers across 132 videos, with 70 reporting a fix. Golfers recommend it for takeaway, release and clubface control and early extension.
  5. Padraig Harrington – Recommended by 331 golfers across 34 videos, with 25 reporting a fix. Golfers recommend it for hip rotation, grip and setup, in a short-tip format.
  6. ChrisRyanGolf – Recommended by 311 golfers across 82 videos, with 33 reporting a fix. Golfers recommend it for takeaway, weight shift and setup, including fixes for the reverse pivot.
  7. Jim Waldron Balance Point Golf – Recommended by 308 golfers across 4 videos, with 59 reporting a fix. Golfers recommend it for backswing, fundamentals and hip rotation. Just four videos draw 308 recommendations, led by The Arm Swing Illusion.
  8. Top Speed Golf - Clay Ballard – Recommended by 288 golfers across 82 videos, with 48 reporting a fix. Golfers recommend it for over-the-top moves, practice drills and the backswing.
  9. Rick Shiels Golf – Recommended by 160 golfers across 34 videos, with 39 reporting a fix. Golfers recommend it for swing fundamentals, grip and setup, in a clear beginner-friendly style.
  10. Titleist – Recommended by 159 golfers across 33 videos, with 9 reporting a fix. Golfers recommend it for weight shift, practice drills and transition.
  11. Kerrod Gray Golf – Recommended by 153 golfers across 45 videos, with 15 reporting a fix. Golfers recommend it for takeaway, setup and weight shift.
  12. Malaska Golf – Recommended by 152 golfers across 48 videos, with 18 reporting a fix. Golfers recommend it for hip rotation, swing fundamentals and practice methods.
  13. PGA Tour – Recommended by 147 golfers across 12 videos, with 13 reporting a fix. Golfers recommend it for transition, practice drills and over-the-top fixes, often with tour players demonstrating.
  14. Meandmygolf – Recommended by 145 golfers across 36 videos, with 15 reporting a fix. Golfers recommend it for transition, grip and setup.
  15. Scratch Golf Academy – Recommended by 142 golfers across 42 videos, with 17 reporting a fix. Golfers recommend it for practice structure, takeaway and release.

What the ranking tells you

Two patterns stand out. First, depth beats fame: some of the most-cited channels are specialist coaches rather than the biggest names. Jim Waldron's channel has just 4 videos in the data and still collects 308 recommendations, while Danny Maude leads for fixes. Second, most top channels are known for the swing itself, particularly the takeaway, transition and hip rotation, which is where amateurs most often get stuck.

Use the list as a starting point, not a verdict. Pick one channel whose style suits you, find the video that matches your specific fault, and give it a few range sessions before moving on. You can browse every problem, from the slice to the putting stroke, to see which videos golfers recommend most for it.

guide_drills.title: The most recommended golf drills (according to golfers)
guide_drills.description: The 15 most recommended golf drill videos, ranked by independent Reddit recommendations and the number of golfers who say they fixed a swing fault.
guide_drills.html:
How we ranked these drills

Drills are easy to find and hard to choose between. GolfVotes ranks drills by how many golfers independently recommended the video on Reddit when somebody asked how to fix a swing fault.

The 15 most recommended drills

  1. Justin Rose shares his feel vs. real swing drill by PGA Tour – Helps with an over-the-top move, by improving hand path and sequencing in transition. Recommended by 86 golfers; 9 say it fixed their problem.
  2. The "Faldo" Pre-Set Drill - Perfect Top of Backswing Position and More... by RollYourRock – Helps with finding a good top-of-backswing position with proper depth and turn. Recommended by 59 golfers; 10 say it fixed their problem.
  3. Best Tiger Woods Golf Swing Drill by TigerWoodsTV – Helps with early extension, by creating space and moving the hips properly in the downswing. Recommended by 34 golfers; 3 say it fixed their problem.
  4. Best ROTATION DRILL for your Backswing and Downswing - It's super SIMPLE! by Danny Maude – Helps with hip turn and weight transfer, especially for armsy swingers. Recommended by 32 golfers; 2 say it fixed their problem.
  5. PERFECT GOLF SWING TAKEAWAY DRILL by Danny Maude – Helps with an inside takeaway that leads to an over-the-top move, by leading with the shoulders. Recommended by 31 golfers; 1 say it fixed their problem.
  6. No Turn Cast Swing Drill by Monte Scheinblum – Helps with casting, by teaching you to feel wrist hinge; it also helps with an overswing. Recommended by 30 golfers; 4 say it fixed their problem.
  7. Simple Drill for a PERFECT TAKEAWAY & WRIST HINGE by Porzak Golf – Helps with takeaway and wrist hinge, built on solid setup fundamentals. Recommended by 30 golfers; 3 say it fixed their problem.
  8. Best TAKEAWAY Drill Ever! by Porzak Golf – Helps with an inside takeaway, using a step to keep lag. Recommended by 27 golfers; 2 say it fixed their problem.
  9. Synchronize Your Golf Swing with the Step Drill by Titleist Tips – Helps with timing of weight shift and rotation, so the body leads the downswing. Recommended by 25 golfers; 1 say it fixed their problem.
  10. Fix Early Extension FAST | Simple Method by Eric Cogorno Golf – Helps with early extension, by keeping the hips back through the swing. Recommended by 22 golfers; 3 say it fixed their problem.
  11. The Towel Drill for backswing arm position by GOLFTEC – Helps with a disconnected backswing, by keeping the arms close to the body; it also works as a warm-up. Recommended by 21 golfers; 2 say it fixed their problem.
  12. HOW TO STOP THE REVERSE PIVOT IN THE BACKSWING by ChrisRyanGolf – Helps with the reverse pivot, with a drill to stop it in the backswing. Recommended by 20 golfers; none have yet reported a fix, but golfers still pass it on.
  13. How to Stay In Posture | The Wall Drill by Top Speed Golf - Clay Ballard – Helps with losing posture through the swing; it also helps shorten an overlong backswing. Recommended by 18 golfers; 3 say it fixed their problem.
  14. Tiger Woods Squat Drill / The Cure for Early Extension (Swing Killer #1) by RollYourRock – Helps with early extension, by clearing the hips and pushing off the trail foot. Recommended by 18 golfers; 2 say it fixed their problem.
  15. [TOUR LIKE BACKSWING] Move Your Right Arm Like THIS by Athletic Motion Golf – Helps with a disconnected trail arm in the backswing, with drills for a tour-like move. Recommended by 16 golfers; 1 say it fixed their problem.

Which drill should you start with?

The list leans heavily toward the takeaway, transition and hips, which is where many amateurs lose their swing. If your ball starts left and curves right, begin with the over-the-top and takeaway drills. If you stand up through impact or hit thin shots, try one of the early extension drills. If you lack lag or power, start with the cast drill and the step drill.

Whichever you choose, do it slowly and check it on video. Carry the feel into real shots, and browse the problem pages for videos matched to your fault.
